name: Sinhala
family: Indo-European, Indo-Iranian, Indo-Aryan (Insular Indo-Aryan, with Dhivehi)
variety: Colloquial (spoken) Sinhala of the Colombo area; the literary language is read with the same sound system
sources: Gair, James W. & Paolillo, John C. (1997). Sinhala. Languages of the World/Materials 34. München: Lincom Europa.
Gair, James W. (2003). Sinhala. In Cardona, George & Jain, Dhanesh (eds.), The Indo-Aryan Languages. London: Routledge.
Karunatillake, W. S. (1992). An Introduction to Spoken Sinhala. Colombo: M. D. Gunasena (3rd edn 2004).
Disanayaka, J. B. (1991). The Structure of Spoken Sinhala. Maharagama: National Institute of Education.
Chandralal, Dileep (2010). Sinhala. London Oriental and African Language Library 15. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Coates, William A. & de Silva, M. W. S. (1960). The segmental phonemes of Sinhalese. University of Ceylon Review 18, 163-175.
Feinstein, Mark (1979). Prenasalization and syllable structure. Linguistic Inquiry 10, 245-278.
Letterman, Rebecca S. (1997). The Effects of Word-Internal Prosody in Sinhala: A Constraint-Based Analysis. PhD dissertation, Cornell University.
Maddieson, Ian & Ladefoged, Peter (1993). Phonetics of partially nasal consonants. In Huffman, Marie K. & Krakow, Rena A. (eds.), Nasals, Nasalization, and the Velum. San Diego: Academic Press.
Ladefoged, Peter & Maddieson, Ian (1996). The Sounds of the World's Languages. Oxford: Blackwell.

Wasala, Asanka; Weerasinghe, Ruvan & Gamage, Kumudu (2006). Sinhala grapheme-to-phoneme conversion and rules for schwa epenthesis. Proceedings of the COLING/ACL 2006 Main Conference Poster Sessions, 890-897.
Masica, Colin P. (1991). The Indo-Aryan Languages. Cambridge University Press.
contrasts: prenasalised voiced stops /ᵐb ⁿd̪ ᶯɖ ᵑɡ/ versus nasal plus stop clusters /mb nd̪ ɳɖ ŋɡ/ (/kaⁿd̪ə/ 'trunk' : /kand̪ə/ 'hill'): one of very few languages with this contrast
no aspiration contrast: only voiced and voiceless stops; the aspirate letters of the script occur in Sanskrit and Pali loans and are read as plain stops
dental versus retroflex stops (the retroflexes are apical and only slightly retracted)
vowel length for all qualities, including the front open vowel /æ/ : /æː/
allophony: prenasalised stops are about as long as a single consonant, with a very short nasal onset, and do not close the preceding syllable; in nasal plus stop clusters the nasal is long and belongs to the preceding syllable

the short open vowel is [a] in the first syllable, before a consonant cluster or geminate, before most word-final consonants and after /h/, and [ə] in other syllables (rules in Wasala et al. 2006, after Karunatillake); forms of the verb /kərənəʋaː/ 'do' have [ə] in the first syllable
word-final nasals are velar [ŋ]; the sign for anusvara is always [ŋ]
/ʋ/ is a labiodental approximant, close to [w] next to back vowels
/r/ is an alveolar tap or short trill
the letters ණ and ළ are pronounced as alveolar [n] and [l]
/ʃ/ is used for both ශ and ෂ in careful speech and is replaced by [s] in casual speech; /f/ is replaced by [p] by some speakers
syllable_structure: (C)V(ː)(C) in native words; clusters occur across syllables and, in loans, initially
phonotactics: prenasalised stops occur only between vowels, not word-initially or word-finally
the inherent vowel of a consonant letter is [a] in the first syllable and mostly [ə] later in the word; a bare consonant is marked with the hal sign
/ə/ does not occur in word-initial syllables except in a few words

stress.rule: Prominence is on the first syllable of the word; heavy syllables (long vowel or closed) resist reduction, which makes them sound prominent too.
stress.cues: vowel quality (full [a] against [ə]) and duration; pitch prominence is phrasal

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: short /a/ is [ə] in light non-initial syllables; other vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: Vowel and consonant quantity both count, so timing has a moraic component; no rhythm metric or measurement of final lengthening could be verified.

length.notes: Seven vowel qualities each short and long (long schwa only in English loans). Geminates and nasal plus stop clusters are roughly twice as long as single consonants and prenasalised stops; I could not verify exact figures.

intonation.declarative: gradual fall to a low ending
intonation.yes_no_question: question particle də after the questioned element; final rise or high-falling ending
intonation.wh_question: wh-word with the particle də, falling ending
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.notes: I know of no instrumental description of Sinhala intonation that I can cite; these entries are impressionistic and of low confidence.

phonation: modal voice only; no breathy voiced or aspirated series in the spoken language

problems: The prenasalised nasals (m#, n#, n.#, N#, n^#) are marked 'temporary' and simply call the full nasals m, n, ɳ, ŋ, ɲ: a prenasalised stop is produced as a full nasal plus stop, so කඳ /kaⁿd̪ə/ and කන්ද /kand̪ə/ sound the same. Only the IPA output shows a difference (ⁿd : nd).
The anusvara sign is [m] unless a velar, palatal or retroflex stop follows: ගං gives [ɡam], මං [mam], සංවිධානය [samwi...]; Sinhala has [ŋ] everywhere.
Word-final ව after a vowel loses its vowel: ලංකාව [laŋkaːw], භාෂාව [bʰaːʃaːw] for [laŋkaːʋə], [baːʃaːʋə]. This affects a very common noun ending.
Aspirate letters are pronounced as aspirated or breathy stops (භ, ධ, ඛ, ඨ), which spoken Sinhala does not have.
/r/ is the English approximant [ɹ] (phoneme r imports base1/r), not a tap.
/a/ becomes [ə] in every unstressed syllable, also in closed ones: මහත්තයා gives [mahəttəjaː] for [mahattəjaː].
ණ and ළ are retroflex [ɳ], [ɭ]; ශ is [s] while ෂ is [ʃ].
The phoneme file notes that its definitions 'are only guesses'; intonation is the reduced generic tune (intonation 2).
good: seven vowel qualities with short and long members, including /æ æː/, at a length ratio of 1 to 2
geminates are produced as double consonants (අම්මා, තාත්තා)
the prenasalised stops are recognised as separate units in the rules and in the IPA output

notes: /f/ and /ʃ/ are loan phonemes; a prenasalised affricate is marginal. The diphthong list is that of Disanayaka 1991 as quoted by Wasala et al. 2006; they can also be treated as vowel plus glide. Four nasalised vowels occur in two or three words only. Maddieson & Ladefoged 1993 give duration measurements for Sinhala prenasalised stops and clusters, but I could not verify the figures, so no numbers are given. No formant or VOT table could be verified either.
